paper_metadata.title: Diffusion tensor analysis of white matter tracts is prognostic of persisting post-concussion symptoms in collegiate athletes

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a subset of a large, well-defined consortium (CARE), but the final sample size is small (n=51) due to significant exclusions (GE scanner incompatibility and missing outcome data). While the source population is clear, the high exclusion rate for technical reasons may introduce selection bias.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The Concussion Assessment, Research and Education (CARE) consortium study enrolled collegiate athletes from 30 sites (NCAA athletic departments and US Department of Defense service academies)
items.reasoning: The source population is clearly defined as collegiate athletes and service academy members within a specific consortium.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Participants with diffusion MRI data were recruited from three Advanced Research Core (ARC) sites: Virginia Tech (VT), University of North Carolina (UNC), and University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).
items.reasoning: The recruitment sites and the specific core (ARC) used for neuroimaging are identified.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: The portion of the CARE dataset used in this study is the first release (CARE 1.0), collected between 2014 and 2018
items.reasoning: The dates of data collection are explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Virginia Tech (VT), University of North Carolina (UNC), and University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).
items.reasoning: Specific academic institutions/geographic locations are provided.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: 51 injuries of concussed athletes scanned within 48 h of injury... All athletes were cleared to return-to-play by the local medical staff following a standardized, graduated protocol.
items.reasoning: The study specifies the timing of the scan (within 48h) and the clinical diagnosis/clearance protocol.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Thirty three injury scans originated from a GE scanner but were not used in the analyses because the intensity values of derivative data were a factor of 2 smaller... Twenty-six injuries had missing return-to-play values
items.reasoning: A large portion of the initial sample (55 out of 106) was excluded due to technical scanner issues or missing data, which may affect how representative the final 51 injuries are.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The 73 injuries belonged to 64 unique athletes (7 with 2 injuries and 2 with 3 injuries), of whom 10 were female and the mean age was 18.85 (±0.85 years).
items.reasoning: Age, sex, and injury count are provided for the baseline sample.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: There is a high rate of missing outcome data (26/73 injuries, ~35%). While the authors list reasons for missingness, they do not provide a comparison of baseline characteristics between those with and without outcome data, making it difficult to rule out informative censoring.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Twenty-six injuries had missing return-to-play values, hence the correlation analysis was limited to 47 injuries
items.reasoning: A loss of over 35% of the eligible Siemens-scanned sample due to missing outcome data is substantial.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper lists reasons for missing data but does not describe active attempts to retrieve missing return-to-play dates for those lost to follow-up.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Missing return to play time points occurs for many reasons, including athletic season ends, athlete transfers, athlete quitting the team, season ending, additional injury... other reasons (e.g. the player is lost to follow-up).
items.reasoning: The authors provide a comprehensive list of reasons for the missing data.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no table or text comparing the characteristics of the 26 excluded injuries to the 47 included injuries.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Without a comparison of the lost-to-follow-up group, it is impossible to determine if they differed systematically from the analyzed group.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (FA and MD) were measured using a highly standardized, automated, and state-of-the-art neuroimaging pipeline (brainlife.io). The methods are reproducible and applied uniformly.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Mean Diffusivity (MD) were estimated for each tract and structure... 30 directions at b-value of 1000 s/mm2 and 8 b0
items.reasoning: The diffusion metrics and the specific MRI parameters are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Data were processed using automated, state-of-the-art, rigorous methods for reproducible data processing using brainlife.io.
items.reasoning: The use of standardized, automated pipelines (QSIPrep, MRtrix3) reduces measurement bias.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: FA and MD were estimated for each tract and structure... Correlation analysis... was then performed
items.reasoning: The study primarily treats the PF as continuous in correlation analyses and uses mean values for classification.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A cutting edge Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) protocol was applied with the goal of identifying advanced biomarkers... Imaging standardization and quality-control procedures were ensured
items.reasoning: A standardized protocol was used across the ARC sites.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: 73 injury scans originated on Siemens scanners and were used for further analysis.
items.reasoning: For the sample selected for analysis, PF data (MRI) was complete.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study did not use imputation; it excluded cases with missing data, which is appropriate for this type of exploratory neuroimaging study, though it impacts power.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (Return-to-Play) is a standard clinical metric in sports medicine, determined by medical staff blinded to the MRI results using a graduated protocol.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: The primary outcome measure is days to clearance of unrestricted return-to-play. Injuries were divided into early (return-to-play < 28 days) and late (return-to-play >= 28 days)
items.reasoning: The outcome and the threshold for 'late recovery' (PPCS) are explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: All athletes were cleared to return-to-play by the local medical staff following a standardized, graduated protocol.
items.reasoning: The use of a standardized clinical protocol by medical staff (who are independent of the imaging analysis) provides a reliable outcome measure.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: following a standardized, graduated protocol.
items.reasoning: The protocol was standardized across the consortium sites.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The authors qualitatively inspected potential confounders (site, sex, sport) and found no obvious outliers, but they did not perform formal multivariable adjustment for these factors in the primary logistic regression model, likely due to the small sample size.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: A qualitative inspection of possible confounding variables of site, sex, number of injuries, and sport type are plotted in eFigure 1.
items.reasoning: Key demographic and injury variables were measured, but other potential confounders like baseline symptom burden or psychological history (mentioned in related work) were not explicitly included in this specific model.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor

items.evidence_snippet: eTable 1 for the demographics table... site, sex, number of injuries, and sport type
items.reasoning: Basic demographic confounders are standard and well-understood.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The CARE dataset... comprises data from cadets and NCAA student-athletes.
items.reasoning: Administrative and clinical records in a prospective consortium are generally reliable for these variables.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: standardized, graduated protocol... CARE consortium structure and methods
items.reasoning: Data collection was standardized across the consortium.

items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: A Logistic Regression binary classifier (LR-BC) was used over individual mean FA tract profiles
items.reasoning: The model used FA tracts as features but did not include age, sex, or site as covariates in the multivariable logistic regression.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods are sophisticated (machine learning with cross-validation), but the very small number of events in the 'Late recovery' group (n=9) puts the model at high risk of overfitting, despite the use of cross-validation. The authors acknowledge this as a significant limitation.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: The dataset was split into a training set (2/3 of the samples) and a test set (1/3 of the samples) using stratified random splits... 5-fold Stratified Cross Validation (CV)
items.reasoning: The machine learning strategy is well-documented.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: the LR-BC was trained also using the mean FA of only the statistically significant tracts identified by the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis
items.reasoning: Selecting variables based on univariate significance (univariate filtering) before multivariable modeling can sometimes lead to optimistic bias, though it is a common practice in high-dimensional neuroimaging data.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Logistic Regression binary classifier (LR-BC)... recommended metrics when dealing with unbalanced datasets, namely Area Under the Curve (AUC), balanced accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.
items.reasoning: Logistic regression is appropriate for binary classification, and the metrics chosen are correct for the class imbalance.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: All processed data derivatives are made available... Jupyter Notebooks used for the statistical analysis, are accessible on brainlife.io
items.reasoning: The high level of transparency and data/code sharing suggests low risk of selective reporting.
